title: Spotting fake login pages
body_md:
## Anyone can hang a sign

It is late, you are tired, and a page says your session has expired. The blue is the right blue, the logo sits where it always sits, and your thumb is already drifting toward the password box. The attack lives in that reflex. A fake login page copies the artwork, the layout and even the error messages, because all it needs is for you to type a password, approve a sign-in or read out a one-time code to someone who controls the page. Some of them wave you on to the real service afterwards, so nothing feels wrong.

A logo is a sign over a shop door, and any painter can make one. What tells you whose shop it is is the street number, and on the web the street number is the address bar.

### Start with how you got here

The way you arrived is the first clue. An unexpected email, an ad, a QR code or a shared document can all drop you on a lookalike site. Read the **address bar** of the browser, not an address printed inside the page, where anyone can write anything. Don’t hold out for a tidy rule such as “the domain must match the brand exactly”: real services run on several domains and often hand sign-in to an outside identity provider. Compare what you see with a bookmark, the app, or a sign-in route you already know. If it looks unfamiliar, stop and ask the service.

HTTPS means the connection to the site in the address bar is encrypted. It says nothing about who runs that site, and scammers get HTTPS too. A missing padlock is a good reason not to type secrets; a padlock that is there is not a good reason to type them.

A password manager can act as an early warning. If it refuses to offer your saved login on a page, find out why. It may be a fake site. It may also be that the manager is locked, the saved address is wrong, the form has changed, or the real service signs you in through a separate identity provider. Either way, don’t type the password by hand to get past the mismatch. Go back by the route you know and ask support if you need to. A manager removes part of the risk, not all of it, particularly if you copy passwords out of it or approve prompts somewhere else.

### The second before you type

Ask yourself: “Did I mean to come to this service, and does this exact sign-in path match what I know?” Stop if the form wants extra personal details, a code you never requested, or your password again after an odd error. None of these proves fraud, because real services sometimes ask for extra verification. Each is a reason to confirm through the account’s usual app or support route.

If you have already typed your password into a page you now doubt, leave it, open the real service on your own, and change the password there, along with every other account where you reused it. Check the active sessions or contact support. If you approved a multi-factor authentication (MFA) request or entered a code, say so when you ask the provider or your workplace security team for help, because what you do next depends on what you gave away. No exercise in this course ever asks for a real password.

widget_config.goal: Before you type credentials, read the real address in the browser and confirm the sign-in route through a path you already know.
widget_config.today_action: Open one of your accounts from its saved app or bookmark. Note the address and how the usual sign-in hands you on. Enter nothing into this lesson.
widget_config.scope: Everyday advice for ordinary users. Sign-in through outside identity providers varies, and recovery steps depend on the service and on workplace policy. The domains in the exercises are invented.

sources.title: UK NCSC: password manager buyers guide
sources.scope: How password managers match saved logins to sites. Written for system owners, and no promise that every fake will be caught.

sources.title: US FTC: public Wi-Fi and HTTPS
sources.scope: Explains that an encrypted scam site can still steal what you type; US consumer context.

sources.title: Gmail Help: avoid and report phishing
sources.scope: Go straight to the service rather than typing a password after a link in a message.

blocks.title: Borrowed branding
blocks.situation: A message that claims to come from a file service sends you to a polished sign-in page at https://files-verify.example/sign-in. It asks for your password and then a one-time code. The browser shows HTTPS.
blocks.analysis: The logo and the encryption vouch for nothing about who runs the page. You came from a message and the address is unfamiliar, and either is reason enough to stop. Close the tab, open the file service from its saved app, and see whether a real notice is waiting there. Never type a code for a sign-in you did not start.

blocks.title: A handoff that is normal
blocks.situation: At work you open the intranet from your saved bookmark, and it passes you to your organization’s usual identity provider. Your password manager offers nothing, because it is locked.
blocks.analysis: A silent password manager does not prove phishing, and this handoff may be your workplace’s ordinary flow. Check it against the documented sign-in route or ask IT through the staff directory. Once that is confirmed, sign in to the manager and let it fill the form. What you should not do is push a password by hand into a form you are unsure of.

blocks.title: The shared project file
blocks.setup: An invented exercise. A colleague seems to have shared a project file with you; the login page is shown here as text only.

steps.prompt: The button in the email opens a page with a familiar logo and HTTPS. What do you do first?

choices.text: Read the browser’s address and remember how you normally reach the file service.
choices.consequence: You ask who will receive the login before you give it.
choices.explanation: The address and the route you know count for more than the artwork.

choices.text: Type your username; the padlock shows who runs the site.
choices.consequence: You start handing details to a site nobody has checked.
choices.explanation: HTTPS protects the trip, not the honesty of whoever runs the site.

steps.prompt: The address is https://team-files-access.example; your usual app signs in somewhere else. What now?

choices.text: Type the password anyway; the file is urgent.
choices.consequence: Your password may land with whoever runs the page.
choices.explanation: A deadline does not settle a doubt about where you are signing in.

choices.text: Close the page and open the file service from your bookmark.
choices.consequence: The unchecked form never sees you.
choices.explanation: Your usual route will show whether anything was really shared.

steps.prompt: Later, the file-service app you normally use shows no file. The colleague is online right now. How do you check?

choices.text: Reply in the same email thread.
choices.consequence: If the mailbox is compromised, the attacker answers.
choices.explanation: Ask the person through a separate channel you already use.

choices.text: Ask the colleague in your usual work chat, or in person.
choices.consequence: You test the claim without going through the email.
choices.explanation: A real colleague can confirm it without the email being involved.

steps.prompt: Suppose you had already typed your password before you stopped. What comes first?

choices.text: Change it in the real service and tell your security or support team what you entered.
choices.consequence: Recovery starts, and the team gets a clear account of what happened.
choices.explanation: Mention any code or approval too, so they can judge how much was exposed.

choices.text: Just close the tab; nothing is lost until a code is entered.
choices.consequence: The password may already be in someone else’s hands.
choices.explanation: Do not wait for proof that it has been misused.

blocks.debrief: A fake page can look exact and be fully encrypted. What worked was going back to the route you know and, once something had been typed, acting on exactly what was exposed. Go through any step again where the page got to set the terms.

questions.prompt: A login page shows HTTPS and your bank’s logo. What does HTTPS actually establish?

choices.text: That the connection to the displayed site is encrypted, not that the site belongs to the bank.
choices.explanation: Whoever runs it may still be a fraudster.

choices.text: That the bank approved the page.
choices.explanation: A certificate secures the connection. It does not confirm the business behind the page.

questions.prompt: You reached a page through a message, and your password manager offers nothing. What is the best response?

choices.text: Type the password by hand, in case it is only a glitch.
choices.explanation: That settles nothing; the mismatch is still unexplained.

choices.text: Stop and reach the account by a route you know.
choices.explanation: Missing autofill is a clue, not a diagnosis, and arriving by your own route settles the question.

questions.prompt: Your bookmarked work site sends you to an identity-provider page you do not recognize. Is it automatically fake?

choices.text: Yes; real sites never redirect you to sign in.
choices.explanation: Legitimate single sign-on often runs on another domain.

choices.text: No; check the handoff against your organization’s documented sign-in flow before you type.
choices.explanation: An unfamiliar route calls for confirmation, not a flat verdict.

questions.prompt: You typed a password into a page you now distrust, but never entered a code. What now?

choices.text: Change it in the real service, ask support for help, and change any copies you reused.
choices.explanation: The password may already be exposed.

choices.text: Do nothing; no code was entered, so there is no harm.
choices.explanation: An exposed password still needs action.
